abstracts.abstract: We introduce a fundamentally new framework for designing online algorithms that we term Adaptive Regret Minimization (ARM). Traditional online algorithms operate under the assumption that the input sequence is adversarial, leading to worst-case bounds that are often overly pessimistic for practical instances. ARM challenges this paradigm by allowing algorithms to dynamically adjust their decision strategies based on detected patterns in the input stream, while maintaining rigorous worst-case guarantees when no patterns are found. Our framework unifies several existing approaches including expert weighting and mirror descent methods under a single theoretical umbrella. We prove that ARM algorithms achieve O(√n) regret in oblivious adversary settings while simultaneously attaining O(log n) regret when inputs exhibit temporal locality—a phenomenon ubiquitous in real-world applications. The key technical contribution is a novel analysis technique called gradient concentration bounds that characterize the tail behavior of cumulative losses under adaptive strategies. We further demonstrate that ARM enables the design of algorithms with smooth trade-offs between adaptability and stability, a dimension absent in classical online learning theory. Computational experiments on online load balancing and web caching problems validate that ARM-based algorithms outperform state-of-the-art methods by factors of 2-5× on correlated input sequences while maintaining competitive performance on adversarial inputs.

We present improved approximation algorithms for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) with distance-constrained customers. The best known prior algorithm achieved a 1.5-approximation ratio using intricate rounding techniques on the standard LP relaxation. Our main result is a 1.4-approximation algorithm that substantially narrows the gap to the integrality gap of 1.25 currently known for the problem. The improvement derives from two technical innovations: first, we introduce a enhanced flow-feasible zone formulation that captures tour structure more accurately than traditional capacity constraints; second, we develop a stratified randomized rounding scheme that respects vehicle capacity limits while reducing the expected tour length. Additionally, we prove that the integrality gap of our enhanced LP is at most 1.35, improving on the previous bound of 1.5. For the special case of uniform capacities, we achieve a 1.33-approximation, the best known ratio for this setting. Our algorithms run in polynomial time using standard convex programming techniques. The analysis relies on a careful coupling argument between the LP solution and the randomized rounding process, which may be of independent interest for related vehicle routing problems. Computational experiments on benchmark instances confirm that our algorithm produces solutions within 1.2× of optimality on average.

We present GraphPipeline, a novel distributed computing framework specifically designed for iterative graph algorithms on massive-scale networks. Existing distributed graph processing systems such as Pregel and Giraph adopt the bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) model, which incurs substantial synchronization overhead and poor load balancing on power-law graphs. GraphPipeline introduces a fully asynchronous execution model augmented with adaptive convergence detection and dynamic workload stealing. The system architecture consists of three novel components: (1) a fine-grained task decomposition engine that partitions vertex-centric computations into micro-tasks of sub-vertex granularity, (2) a lock-free progress tracking mechanism using epoch-based reclamation that enables lock-free coordination among workers, and (3) a machine-learning-guided work stealing policy that predicts straggler vertices and proactively migrates their computations. We implement GraphPipeline in Rust using Apache Arrow for zero-copy data interchange and deploy it on clusters of up to 512 machines. Our evaluation on real-world graphs with billions of edges demonstrates that GraphPipeline achieves speedups of 10-50× over Giraph and PowerGraph on typical iterative algorithms including PageRank, connected components, and label propagation. The system maintains linear scalability up to 256 workers and exhibits graceful degradation on heterogeneous hardware. GraphPipeline is released as open-source software with full compatibility with the existing Giraph API.

We describe a highly optimized implementation of cache-oblivious algorithms for exact string matching on modern processor architectures. Prior cache-oblivious string matching algorithms achieved theoretical optimality but suffered from poor practical performance due to branch mispredictions, poor instruction-level parallelism, and suboptimal cache behavior on real hardware. Our system, called CacheString, incorporates three key optimizations: (1) a cache-oblivious tournament tree structure that reduces branch mispredictions by 94% compared to previous approaches, (2) SIMD vectorization of the inner loop achieving 16-way parallelism on AVX-512 processors, and (3) a hybrid memory access pattern that combines the theoretical benefits of cache-obliviousness with cache-aware prefetching heuristics. We further present a cache-oblivious dynamic programming framework for edit distance computation that achieves a 8× speedup over the previous best implementation by exploiting memory bandwidth more effectively. Extensive experiments on genomic sequences, natural language texts, and binary data demonstrate that CacheString outperforms optimized SIMD implementations such as SWIPE and YARA by factors of 2-4× while using less memory. The system achieves near-peak memory bandwidth utilization (85-92%) on Intel Skylake and AMD Zen2 processors. Source code is provided under an open-source license, and our optimization techniques are applicable to a broader class of cache-oblivious algorithms.
